name: secure-web-app
description: Hardened baseline for applications generated by SecureVibe: a server-rendered Node.js/Express app with local accounts, admin two-factor sign-in, strict input checking, safe defaults for headers, sessions and cookies, encrypted sensitive fields, tamper-evident audit logging and a security test suite. Every control below is verified again on the generated code, so the compliance report only credits controls that are still in place.

features.description: User accounts with sign-in, sign-out, password change and reset, and roles. Always on in this template version.
Administrators must set up an authenticator app (time-based one-time codes) on first sign-in.
Every user may add an authenticator app to their account.
File uploads with type checks, size limits, random file names and owner-only downloads.
A Claude-backed assistant with input screening, output checks, logging, budgets and a kill switch.
The assistant may propose actions from a fixed tool list; a person must confirm each one before it runs.
features.note: The tool code ships with the assistant (context.ts and index.ts import it); this flag only decides whether actions are offered.

features.description: A separate classification call scores assistant inputs and outputs for harmful content.
The assistant remembers the conversation per user; the user can reset it.
Outgoing email (notifications, reset links) through SMTP; locally, mail is written to a file outbox instead.
Background jobs declared in code, run one at a time with a lock so they never overlap.
API keys so other programs can call the JSON API on behalf of a user.
A placeholder checkout page and a guide for a provider-hosted payment flow. Card numbers are never stored.
Sensitive database fields are encrypted with a key that lives only in the environment.
A scheduled job deletes or pseudonymises old personal data according to the retention policy.
The app calls other web services, only through the allow-listed outbound client.
The reference "notes" feature that shows every convention. Off in production.

controls.title: Nonce-based Content Security Policy with the exact contract policy
controls.description: Every page tells the browser exactly which scripts and styles are allowed to run, using a fresh random nonce per request. Injected scripts are blocked even if an attacker manages to place text on a page.

asvs.proves: Every response carries a Content-Security-Policy with a per-request nonce, strict-dynamic, object-src none and base-uri none, so unexpected scripts and plugins cannot run.
The policy sets frame-ancestors to none, so the pages cannot be embedded in another site.

controls.title: nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP and CORP headers
controls.description: Browsers are told not to guess file types, not to leak page addresses to other sites, not to use the camera, microphone or location, and to keep this app isolated from other open pages.

asvs.proves: Every response carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so browsers never reinterpret a response as a different type.
Every response carries Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy.

controls.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security for at least one year (TLS modes)
controls.description: When the app is served over HTTPS, browsers are told to keep using HTTPS for a year, so a later visit cannot be downgraded to plain HTTP.

asvs.proves: In TLS modes every response carries Strict-Transport-Security with max-age of at least 31536000 and includeSubDomains.

controls.title: Content-Type with charset on every response
controls.description: Every answer states its type and character set, so browsers never have to guess how to interpret it.

asvs.proves: Every response with a body has a Content-Type header that includes charset=utf-8, for pages, JSON and error responses alike.

controls.title: No cross-origin resource sharing; Origin never reflected
controls.description: Other websites cannot read data from this app through the browser, because the app never grants cross-site access.

asvs.proves: No CORS middleware is installed and a foreign Origin header is never reflected in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, including on preflight requests.

controls.title: No caching of signed-in pages
controls.description: Pages shown to a signed-in user are marked so browsers and shared proxies do not keep a copy that someone else could see later.

asvs.proves: Every response to an authenticated request carries Cache-Control: no-store, private.

controls.title: Session cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict; the session id lives only in the cookie
controls.description: The sign-in cookie cannot be read by scripts in the browser and is not sent along with requests started by other websites.

asvs.proves: The session cookie is set with HttpOnly, so page scripts cannot read it.
The session cookie is set with SameSite=Strict, so cross-site requests never carry it.

controls.title: Secure flag and __Host- prefix on the session cookie (TLS modes)
controls.description: When the app runs over HTTPS, the sign-in cookie is only ever sent over the encrypted connection and cannot be overwritten from another sub-domain.

asvs.proves: In TLS modes the session cookie carries the Secure attribute.
In TLS modes the session cookie is named __Host-sid with Path=/ and no Domain, so it is host-bound.

controls.title: TLS 1.2 or newer with modern ciphers (self-signed mode)
controls.description: When the app serves HTTPS itself, it refuses old, breakable encryption versions.

asvs.proves: The built-in HTTPS server only negotiates TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
The built-in HTTPS server uses Node's modern cipher defaults and rejects legacy cipher suites.

controls.title: Cross-site request forgery protection on every state-changing route
controls.description: A form or request that changes something must carry a secret token tied to the user's session and must come from this app's own pages. Reading pages never changes data.

asvs.proves: State-changing requests without a valid synchronizer token, or with a foreign Origin or cross-site Sec-Fetch-Site header, are rejected with 403 before any change happens.
GET requests never change state; logout and other mutations only work as POST with a token.

controls.title: Clear-Site-Data on logout
controls.description: When a user signs out, the browser is told to delete this site's cookies and stored data, so nothing is left behind on a shared computer.

asvs.proves: The logout response carries Clear-Site-Data: "cookies", "storage".

controls.title: No hidden files, no directory listings, no source or configuration served
controls.description: The web server only hands out the public CSS and JavaScript files. Configuration, source code and hidden files are never reachable from a browser.

asvs.proves: Requests for dotfiles, .git, .env, package files and source code get 403/404, and directories are not listed.
Only the public/ folder is served statically; the application tree is never exposed.

controls.title: TRACE method not supported
controls.description: The diagnostic TRACE request type, which can echo back cookies, is refused.

asvs.proves: A TRACE request is answered with 405 and never echoed.

controls.title: Minimal health endpoints; readiness only from the local machine
controls.description: The health check says only "ok" and reveals nothing about versions or internals. The readiness check is only reachable from the machine the app runs on unless it was deliberately opened to the network.

asvs.proves: /healthz returns only {"status":"ok"} and /readyz returns only a status field and is loopback-only unless BIND_LAN=1.

controls.title: Generic error responses that fail closed
controls.description: When something goes wrong the user sees a short, friendly message with the right status code. Technical details stay in the server log, and an error never accidentally shows protected content.

asvs.proves: 404, 400 and 500 responses are the uniform error model with no stack traces, SQL text or file paths, in both page and JSON form.
The last-resort error handler always answers with an error response, never with partially rendered protected content.

controls.title: Request body limits, simple query parsing, parameter and prototype pollution rejected
controls.description: Oversized requests are refused before they are processed, repeated or nested query parameters are never turned into arrays or objects, and special keys that could change how JavaScript objects behave are rejected.

asvs.proves: Bodies larger than the configured limit are rejected with 413 and JSON bodies with __proto__ or constructor.prototype keys are rejected with 400.
The query parser is set to simple, so duplicate parameters never become arrays and bracket syntax never becomes objects.

controls.title: Strict server-side schemas on every route
controls.description: Every route declares exactly which fields it accepts and what type each must be. Anything extra, missing or of the wrong type is refused with a clear message before the app touches it.

asvs.proves: Every route's params, query and body are validated server-side against strict zod schemas registered in the route registry.
Validation is positive (allow-list): unknown fields are rejected with 400 rather than stripped or ignored.
Type-strict schemas reject arrays where scalars are expected and numbers where strings are expected.
Strict object schemas prevent mass assignment: fields not in the schema never reach the data layer.

controls.title: Validation rules documented from the schemas
controls.description: The list of accepted fields and rules for every route is generated from the code itself, so the documentation cannot drift from reality.

asvs.proves: docs/validation.md, regenerated from the route schemas, documents the input validation rules per route.
docs/validation.md lists every accepted field per route with its type and limits.

controls.title: Serializers shape every response; raw database rows are never returned
controls.description: Before data is sent to a browser it passes through a function that picks only the fields that audience may see. Password hashes, encrypted values and internal ids never leave the server by accident.

asvs.proves: JSON and page responses only contain fields chosen by toPublicDto/toOwnerDto/toAdminDto; hashes, secrets and encrypted blobs are absent.
Field-level shaping per audience (public, owner, admin) is enforced by the serializers.

controls.title: Deny-by-default route registry; anonymous and wrong-role access refused on the server
controls.description: No page or API route exists without a stated rule for who may use it. Visitors who are not signed in, or who have the wrong role, are refused by the server itself, not just hidden in the menu.

asvs.proves: Every route is registered with an explicit auth value and the server denies anonymous and wrong-role requests with 401/403/404 before the handler runs.
Authorization is decided on the server from the session; client-side hints such as role fields or headers are ignored.

sbd.proves: Role-based access control with least privilege is enforced centrally by the route registry.

controls.title: Ownership enforced for records that belong to a user
controls.description: A user can only open, change or delete their own records, even if they guess the address of someone else's.

asvs.proves: Routes declared with an owner rule load the record and compare its owner to the signed-in user; another user's record yields 403/404 (admins may bypass only where declared).

controls.title: Access rules documented from the route registry
controls.description: The who-may-do-what table is generated from the route declarations, so it always matches the running app.

asvs.proves: docs/authorization.md, regenerated from the route registry, documents the access rule of every route.
docs/authorization.md documents which routes are owner-scoped and which roles may bypass ownership.

controls.title: Password policy: length 12 to 256, no composition rules, breached-password and context-word checks
controls.description: Passwords must be at least 12 characters, may be anything the user likes (spaces, symbols, long phrases), and are refused if they are on a list of commonly used passwords or contain the user's own name or email.

asvs.proves: Passwords shorter than 12 characters are rejected and 12 characters are accepted.
Passwords found in the bundled common-password list are rejected.
No character-composition rules are imposed; any mix of characters is accepted.
Passwords are verified exactly as entered without trimming, truncation or case folding.
Passwords of at least 64 characters (up to 256) are accepted and used in full.
Passwords containing context words such as the account name or email local part are rejected.
docs/SECURITY.md states the password policy that the code enforces.

controls.title: Changing a password requires the current password
controls.description: Nobody can set a new password on an account they happen to find signed in without proving they know the current one.

asvs.proves: Users can change their own password through the account page.
The change-password form requires the correct current password; a wrong one leaves the password unchanged.

controls.title: Password fields are masked and allow pasting
controls.description: Password boxes hide what is typed and let people paste from a password manager.

asvs.proves: All password inputs are rendered as type="password" with autocomplete hints.
Password inputs never block paste (no onpaste handlers or paste-blocking scripts).

controls.title: Approved password hashing parameters (argon2id or scrypt)
controls.description: Stored passwords are turned into slow, salted hashes that are impractical to reverse even if the database is copied.

asvs.proves: Passwords are stored as PHC strings from argon2id (m=65536,t=3,p=4) when available, otherwise scrypt (N=131072,r=8,p=1,keylen=64).
The password hash parameters match the approved configuration and the startup log records the active algorithm.

controls.title: Sign-in anti-automation: per-account and per-address limits, backoff, soft lock, uniform responses
controls.description: Repeated wrong sign-in attempts slow down and then pause an account temporarily, without locking anyone out permanently. Responses never reveal whether an email address has an account.

asvs.proves: After 5 failures in 15 minutes an account is soft-locked with 429 and Retry-After, per-ip limits apply, unknown users are answered identically with a dummy hash verification, and the lock is never permanent.
The sign-in route is rate limited per account and per client address with exponential backoff.

sbd.proves: Sign-in has rate limiting and back-off so brute-force traffic cannot exhaust the app.

controls.title: No default accounts; bootstrap admin with a random one-time password
controls.description: A fresh installation has no accounts at all. The first administrator gets a random password shown once, must change it at first sign-in, and it expires after a day if unused.

asvs.proves: A fresh production database contains no accounts and well-known default credentials never sign in.
The bootstrap admin receives a random 16-byte one-time password with must_change_password set and a 24-hour expiry.

controls.title: No password hints or secret questions
controls.description: The app never asks for or shows password hints or "security questions", which are easy to guess.

asvs.proves: No sign-in, reset, registration or account page contains hint or secret-question fields.

controls.title: Password reset with a hashed, short-lived, single-use random token
controls.description: A reset link contains a long random code that works once, for 15 minutes, and is stored only as a hash. The reply to a reset request is the same whether or not the address has an account, and an authenticator app is still required afterwards.

asvs.proves: Reset tokens are single use, expire after 15 minutes, the response is identical for unknown accounts, and TOTP is still required after a reset.
Reset tokens are 16 CSPRNG bytes (128 bits) and are stored only as HMAC-SHA256(TOKEN_HMAC_KEY, token).
A password reset never bypasses the second factor for enrolled accounts.

controls.title: Anti-automation and security contact documented
controls.description: docs/SECURITY.md explains the sign-in limits and who to contact about a security problem, generated from the real settings.

asvs.proves: docs/SECURITY.md, regenerated from the rate-limit presets, documents the anti-automation controls on authentication.
docs/SECURITY.md documents the sign-in, reset and registration protections and their limits.

controls.title: No forced password rotation
controls.description: Users are not forced to change their password on a schedule, which leads to weaker passwords; they change it when there is a reason to.

asvs.proves: No password expiry column, setting or check exists; old passwords remain valid until the user changes them.

controls.title: Authenticator-app codes (TOTP) with an encrypted random seed and replay protection
controls.description: The second sign-in step uses standard six-digit codes from an authenticator app. The secret behind the codes is random, stored encrypted, and each code works only once within its short time window.

asvs.proves: TOTP codes are accepted only once; a replayed code is rejected.
Enrolment generates a 20-byte CSPRNG seed that is stored encrypted with the field key.
Codes follow RFC 6238 with a 30-second step and at most one step of drift; older codes are rejected.

controls.title: Recovery codes: ten random codes, stored hashed, each usable once
controls.description: When someone sets up the authenticator app they get ten backup codes for when the phone is lost. Each works once and the app stores only hashes of them.

asvs.proves: Recovery codes are shown once, stored hashed and each code is invalidated after use.
Each recovery code is 10 base32 characters (50 bits) from a CSPRNG and all ten are unique.

controls.title: Second-factor verification is rate limited
controls.description: Guessing six-digit codes is stopped after a handful of tries.

asvs.proves: The MFA step allows at most 5 attempts per account in 15 minutes and answers 429 with Retry-After beyond that.

controls.title: Second factor required for administrators and available to everyone
controls.description: Administrators cannot use the app until they have set up an authenticator app. Every other user can turn it on from their account page. An administrator can reset a user's second factor, and the reason is logged.

asvs.proves: Admin accounts get no usable session from the password alone and MFA enrolment is offered on the account pages of every user.
An administrator can reset a user's second factor through a logged action that records a reason.

sbd.proves: Multi-factor authentication is enforced for administrators; there is no central identity provider, so this coverage is partial.

controls.title: Random 256-bit session references verified on the server and stored hashed
controls.description: The sign-in cookie holds only a long random reference. Everything about the session is kept on the server, and the reference is stored as a keyed hash so a copied database cannot be used to hijack sessions.

asvs.proves: Sessions are reference tokens: the cookie value carries no user data and all state is server-side.
Session ids are 32 CSPRNG bytes encoded as base64url.
Session ids are validated against the server-side store and stored only as HMAC-SHA256(SESSION_SECRET, id).

controls.title: New session id on sign-in; the old id stops working
controls.description: Signing in always issues a fresh session reference, so a reference planted before sign-in can never be upgraded.

asvs.proves: The session id is regenerated on login (and on MFA verification) and the previous id is revoked.

controls.title: Idle and absolute session timeouts from configuration, documented
controls.description: A session ends after a period of inactivity and, no matter what, after a maximum lifetime. The values come from the configuration and are written into the documentation.

asvs.proves: A session past SESSION_IDLE_MINUTES of inactivity is rejected server-side.
A session older than SESSION_ABSOLUTE_HOURS is rejected even while active.
docs/sessions.md, regenerated from the session constants, documents the timeouts.

controls.title: Sign-out ends the session on the server
controls.description: After signing out, the old cookie is useless even if someone copied it.

asvs.proves: Logout revokes the session record; reusing the old cookie is rejected.

controls.title: Disabling or deleting an account ends all of its sessions
controls.description: When an administrator disables or deletes an account, the person is signed out everywhere at once.

asvs.proves: Disabling or deleting a user calls revokeAllForUser, so every existing session is rejected afterwards and the account cannot sign in.

controls.title: "Log out everywhere" on password change; administrators can end a user's sessions
controls.description: When a password is changed the user can end all other sessions, and an administrator can end all sessions of any user.

asvs.proves: The change-password form offers a log-out-everywhere option that revokes the other sessions.
An administrator can revoke all sessions of a user and a session.revoked event is recorded.

controls.title: Sign-out available on every signed-in page
controls.description: Every page shown to a signed-in user has a sign-out button in the layout.

asvs.proves: The base layout renders a logout form on every authenticated page.

controls.title: Re-authentication before sensitive account changes; session list and revoke
controls.description: Changing the email address or the authenticator settings requires entering the password (and code) again within the last five minutes. Users can see their active sessions and end any of them.

asvs.proves: Email and MFA changes are refused unless the user re-authenticated within 5 minutes.
The account pages list active sessions with created, last seen and address, and allow revoking any of them.

controls.title: Limit on concurrent sessions per user
controls.description: A user can be signed in on a limited number of devices; the oldest session is ended when the limit is exceeded.

asvs.proves: SESSION_MAX_CONCURRENT is enforced by revoking the oldest session and is documented in docs/sessions.md.

controls.title: Only parameterised database queries through the wrapper
controls.description: Data is never pasted into database commands as text. Every query goes through one wrapper that keeps values separate from the command, which rules out SQL injection.

asvs.proves: All SQL goes through the db wrapper with bound parameters; no string-built SQL exists in the code base.

controls.title: Safe database settings, private files, transactions and bounded lists
controls.description: The database uses safe settings, its files are readable only by the app's user, related writes happen all-or-nothing, and lists are always limited in size.

asvs.proves: Per-user quotas are checked inside a transaction and list queries always carry a LIMIT.
Database and data-directory files are created with mode 0600/0700 and secure_delete, so stored records are protected from other local users.

controls.title: Field encryption with AES-256-GCM, versioned keys and rotation
controls.description: Sensitive fields are encrypted before they are stored, with a key that lives only in the environment. Keys are numbered so they can be rotated, and tampering with stored values is detected.

asvs.proves: Sensitive fields are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, an authenticated mode.
Ciphertexts use the versioned v<keyId>:iv:tag:ct format with a fresh random 12-byte IV per value and AAD bound to table, column and row.
A tampered ciphertext or tag fails authentication and is rejected instead of decrypted.
Keys are versioned in FIELD_KEYS; a new active key is used for new data and rotate-field-key re-encrypts old data.
Keys are loaded from the environment only and never stored in the database or code.

sbd.proves: Sensitive data at rest is encrypted with rotatable keys; in-transit protection depends on the TLS mode.

controls.title: Only built-in, approved cryptography
controls.description: All encryption, hashing and random numbers come from Node's built-in crypto library; weak or home-made algorithms are not used anywhere.

asvs.proves: No MD5 or SHA-1 is used in a security context and no third-party or custom crypto libraries are imported.
Only node:crypto primitives (randomBytes, HMAC-SHA256, AES-256-GCM, argon2id/scrypt) are used; Math.random never appears in security code.

controls.title: Cryptography inventory documented
controls.description: A generated document lists every place the app uses encryption, hashing or keys, and how keys are managed.

asvs.proves: docs/crypto.md, regenerated from crypto-inventory.json, lists the algorithms, key sizes and where they are used.
docs/crypto.md documents key ownership, storage in the environment and the rotation command.

controls.title: Secrets from the environment only, strength checked, placeholders refused
controls.description: Passwords, keys and secrets are never written in the code. The app refuses to start when a secret is missing, too short, or still the example value.

asvs.proves: SESSION_SECRET, FIELD_KEYS and TOKEN_HMAC_KEY must decode to at least 32 bytes and differ from the .env.example placeholders, or startup fails naming the variable.
Secrets are read from the environment (.env) with strict file permissions and never from source code or the database.

sbd.proves: Secrets are generated strong and kept out of code and logs; there is no secret manager, so this is partial.

controls.title: Structured JSON logs with UTC time, request id, user, route and outcome
controls.description: Every log line is a machine-readable record with the time, a request id to follow one request end to end, who acted, on which route, and whether it succeeded.

asvs.proves: Every log entry is JSON with a UTC ISO timestamp, reqId, userId when known, route and outcome.
Log entries include the request id, source address and user so events across requests can be correlated.
Timestamps are UTC ISO 8601 so events from different sources line up.

sbd.proves: Structured logs with correlation ids make requests traceable.

controls.title: Redaction: no passwords, tokens, cookies or raw session ids in logs
controls.description: Sensitive values are removed before anything is written to the log, and session ids appear only as a short hash prefix.

asvs.proves: Redaction paths cover password*, *token*, authorization, cookie, set-cookie, totp*, *secret*, *apiKey* and sensitive entity fields; session ids are logged as the first 8 characters of their hash.

controls.title: Security events for sign-in, denied access, rejected input, rate limits and unexpected errors
controls.description: Important security moments are recorded as named events so an administrator can see failed sign-ins, blocked requests and errors.

asvs.proves: Authentication successes and failures are logged with the factor used and the failure reason.
Validation rejections, CSRF rejections and rate-limit hits are logged as security events.
Authorization denials are logged with route, user and resource.
Unexpected errors are logged as error.unhandled with the request id.

sbd.proves: Security-relevant actions, including administrative actions, produce structured events.

controls.title: Log injection prevented by JSON encoding
controls.description: Text supplied by users cannot create fake log lines, because every entry is encoded as JSON.

asvs.proves: Newlines and JSON-like text in user input stay inside one encoded JSON string and never form a separate log entry.

controls.title: Append-only, hash-chained audit table with a verify command and retention setting
controls.description: Security events are also written to an audit table where each entry is linked to the previous one by a hash. A command checks the chain, so tampering with past records is detectable. Records are kept for a configurable period (default 400 days) and deleted users are pseudonymised.

asvs.proves: The audit_log table is append-only with prev_hash/hash chaining and audit:verify detects any modified or removed row.

sbd.proves: Audit records are tamper-evident locally and retained for AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 400); shipping them to a separate system is a deployment step.
Administrative actions are recorded in the audit table with actor, time and outcome.

controls.title: Logging documented from the event catalog
controls.description: The list of logged events and the log format are generated from the code, so the documentation matches what the app really records.

asvs.proves: docs/logging.md, regenerated from the event catalog, documents which events are logged and why.
docs/logging.md documents the log format, fields, redaction and retention.

controls.title: Rate limits on registration, password reset, the assistant, uploads and general traffic
controls.description: Automated abuse of sign-up, reset, uploads and the assistant is slowed down, and any single client is limited in how many requests per minute it can make.

asvs.proves: Registration (3/hour per ip), reset (3/hour per account, 10/hour per ip), ai, uploads and general (300/min per ip) presets answer 429 with Retry-After and emit ratelimit.hit.

sbd.proves: Rate limits and per-user quotas are applied at the application edge.

controls.title: Client address taken only from configured proxy hops
controls.description: The app trusts the real network address of the caller, not a header a caller can forge, unless it has been told it sits behind a known proxy.

asvs.proves: With TRUST_PROXY_HOPS=0 the X-Forwarded-For header is ignored for rate limiting and logging.
The trust-proxy setting is an explicit hop count from configuration, never true.

controls.title: Outbound calls only to allow-listed hosts, with timeouts, size caps, manual redirects and a circuit breaker
controls.description: The app can only talk to the outside services it was told about. Each call has a time limit and a size limit, redirects are not followed blindly, certificates are always checked, and a failing service is paused instead of hanging the app.

asvs.proves: Outbound URLs are restricted to OUTBOUND_ALLOWED_HOSTS, so user-influenced targets cannot reach internal or arbitrary hosts (SSRF).
Every outbound request goes through outboundFetch, which denies hosts not on the allow-list and emits outbound.blocked.
Outbound requests have a 10-second timeout and a 1 MB response cap.
Outbound redirects are returned to the caller (redirect: manual), never followed automatically.
TLS certificate validation is never disabled for outbound connections.
A circuit breaker opens after repeated failures so the app degrades gracefully instead of waiting on a failing service.

sbd.proves: External dependencies are wrapped in a circuit breaker with a degraded mode.
Outbound failures are handled with timeouts and back-off instead of cascading.

controls.title: Outbound connections documented
controls.description: A generated document lists every outside service the app talks to and how those connections are protected.

asvs.proves: docs/communications.md, regenerated from OUTBOUND_ALLOWED_HOSTS and the http-client settings, documents every outbound connection.

controls.title: Redirects only to allow-listed local paths
controls.description: After sign-in or other actions the app only ever sends the browser to its own pages, never to an address an attacker put in a link.

asvs.proves: safeRedirect only accepts relative local paths from an allow-list; external hosts, protocol-relative and scheme URLs fall back to the default page.
Redirect targets are validated and the Location header is a single well-formed value, so header injection through redirects is prevented.

controls.title: Auto-escaped templates, no unescaped user data, no inline scripts
controls.description: Everything shown on a page is escaped so text from users is displayed as text and never runs as code. Scripts live in separate files and carry the per-request nonce.

asvs.proves: EJS <%= %> output encoding is used for all data; <%- %> only appears for the nonce, CSRF token or safeHtml() results.
Output encoding happens in the view layer for the HTML context, consistently across every template.
No inline scripts or event handlers exist in views; scripts come from public/js with the CSP nonce.

controls.title: No eval, Function or vm
controls.description: The app never turns text into running code.

asvs.proves: No eval, new Function or node:vm usage exists anywhere in the application code.

controls.title: Upload size cap enforced while streaming
controls.description: A file larger than the allowed size is cut off as it arrives, before it fills up disk or memory.

asvs.proves: busboy limits fileSize to UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES and the request is aborted with 413 when exceeded.

controls.title: File type checked by content, extension and declared type; risky types refused
controls.description: The app looks inside each uploaded file to confirm what it really is, checks that the name and declared type agree, and refuses types that can carry scripts (SVG, HTML, XML, ZIP).

asvs.proves: The first 16 bytes are matched against a magic table; the sniffed type must be allow-listed and consistent with the extension and declared Content-Type, else 415.
SVG, HTML, XML and ZIP uploads are always refused, so no user-supplied markup or archives are processed.

controls.title: Random file names, stored outside the web folder, private permissions
controls.description: Uploaded files are saved under random names in a private folder that the web server never serves directly, and the name a user gave is never used as a path.

asvs.proves: Files are stored as DATA_DIR/uploads/<uuid> with mode 0600; the original name is kept only as sanitised metadata.
Uploads are stored outside public/ and are never served as static files.

controls.title: Downloads sent as attachments with safe headers and the stored type
controls.description: Downloaded files are offered for saving rather than displayed, with headers that stop browsers from guessing the type or running anything inside the file.

asvs.proves: Downloads use the Content-Type stored in the database, never the request or extension.
Downloads carry Content-Disposition: attachment with an RFC 6266 encoded name, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Content-Security-Policy: sandbox and Cache-Control: private, no-store.
Download responses declare a safe Content-Type with nosniff so the browser cannot reinterpret them.

controls.title: Owner-only downloads and per-user upload quota
controls.description: Only the person who uploaded a file (or an administrator) can download it, and each user has a limit on how many files and how much space they may use.

asvs.proves: The download route is registered with an owner rule so other users get 403/404.
Per-user count and byte quotas are enforced inside a transaction before a file is accepted.

controls.title: Upload rules documented
controls.description: A generated document states the allowed file types, size limits and quotas.

asvs.proves: docs/uploads.md, regenerated from the upload configuration, documents the allowed types, limits and storage.

controls.title: Assistant input normalised; control characters and reserved model tokens refused
controls.description: Text sent to the assistant is cleaned into a standard form. Hidden control characters and special sequences that models treat as commands are refused before anything reaches the model.

aisvs.proves: Input is NFKC-normalised and Unicode format/control characters are stripped before validation.
Only printable text plus newline and tab is accepted; remaining control characters cause a 400/422.
Reserved sequences such as <|, |>, [INST] and <<SYS>> are refused and logged as ai.input.rejected.

controls.title: Encoded smuggling and over-long input rejected, never truncated
controls.description: Long runs of encoded text that could hide instructions are refused, and messages over the size limit are rejected outright rather than silently cut.

aisvs.proves: Base64 or hex runs longer than 200 characters are rejected.
Input longer than AI_MAX_INPUT_CHARS is rejected with 422 and is never truncated or sent to the model.

controls.title: Prompt-injection screening with blocking and logging
controls.description: Messages are compared with a list of known manipulation patterns. Clear attempts are blocked and recorded; suspicious ones are flagged.

aisvs.proves: High-precision injection patterns block the request with ai.input.rejected; medium patterns continue with ai.input.flagged.
Every blocked or flagged input produces a security event with the rule that matched.

controls.title: Instruction hierarchy, untrusted-data wrapping and user-scoped data access
controls.description: The assistant's fixed instructions outrank anything a user types. Data pulled from the app is wrapped as untrusted content and only ever comes from records the signed-in user is allowed to see.

aisvs.proves: The hash-pinned system prompt states the instruction hierarchy and user text cannot override it.
App data reaches the model only through repository functions scoped to req.user, wrapped in <untrusted_data> blocks and screened.
Untrusted content is delimited and screened with the same ruleset as user input before it enters the context.
The assistant acts with the signed-in user's authorization only; it never gains data access beyond that user.

controls.title: Assistant output checked against a schema, bounded, filtered and shown as plain text
controls.description: Replies must match an expected shape and length, must not repeat the assistant's hidden instructions, must not mention records the user cannot see, and are shown as plain text so nothing in them can run.

aisvs.proves: Model output is validated against the {answer, refused, reason} schema; invalid output is replaced by the fallback message and logged as ai.output.rejected.
Answers are bounded to 4000 characters and AI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS.
An n-gram overlap check blocks replies that disclose the system prompt.
Replies are rendered as escaped text with no markdown-to-HTML or auto-linking, and a post-inference filter removes ids and emails of records the user may not access.

controls.title: Every assistant interaction logged with token usage, attributed per user, session and endpoint, with budgets
controls.description: Each assistant request is recorded with the model used, how much it cost in tokens and hashes of the prompt and reply. Usage is counted per person so daily budgets can be enforced.

aisvs.proves: Every request emits ai.request and inserts an ai_interactions row with user, session hash, model, provider, operation, token counts and prompt/response hashes.
Logged interactions include the session context and whether injection screening flagged the input.
AI log entries follow a fixed structured schema with model id, token usage, provider and operation.
Token usage is attributed per user, per session and per endpoint in the ai_usage table.
A per-user daily token budget is enforced with 429 and ai.budget.exceeded.
Per-user token accounting provides the usage records for cost and abuse monitoring.

controls.title: Assistant kill switch: environment flag and administrator toggle, both logged
controls.description: The assistant can be switched off instantly with a setting or by an administrator in the app. Users then see a plain "not available" message, and the switch is recorded.

aisvs.proves: AI_ENABLED=0 or the admin runtime toggle stops inference with 503 on every request.
Every kill-switch change emits ai.killswitch.toggled with the acting administrator.

controls.title: API key never in the model context; pinned model documented
controls.description: The key that pays for the assistant is never included in anything sent to the model, and the exact model version in use is listed in a generated document.

aisvs.proves: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is read only by the SDK client and never appears in prompts, tools or logs.
docs/ai.md records the pinned AI_MODEL, provider and configured limits as the model inventory.
The vendor-hosted model is pinned by id in configuration and documented in docs/ai.md.

controls.title: Conversation memory belongs to one user and can be reset
controls.description: What the assistant remembers is stored per person; nobody else can see it and the user can clear it at any time.

aisvs.proves: ai_conversations rows are scoped to user_id and every read filters by the signed-in user.
POST /ai/reset deletes the user's stored conversation history.

controls.title: Content moderation on assistant input and output
controls.description: A separate check scores messages and replies for harmful content and blocks those above the configured threshold, recording each decision.

aisvs.proves: Inputs are classified for violence, self-harm, hate and sexual content and rejected above the threshold with ai.moderation.decision logged.
Outputs are classified with the same categories and blocked above the threshold.

controls.title: Assistant actions: fixed tool list, validated inputs, human confirmation, normal authorization
controls.description: The assistant can only suggest actions from a short fixed list. Anything that changes data becomes a proposal the user must confirm, and the app then runs it with the user's own permissions. The model never executes anything itself.

aisvs.proves: Tools are a fixed allow-list in src/features/ai/tools.ts; mutating tools return a proposal that requires POST /ai/confirm/:proposalId with CSRF.
Tool inputs and outputs are validated against zod schemas and invalid proposals are refused at execution.
A confirmed action executes through the normal repository functions with req.user authorization, never through the model.
Proposals are bound to the user who created them; another user cannot confirm them.

controls.title: Mail headers sanitised; templates only from disk
controls.description: Text from users cannot add extra recipients or headers to outgoing email, and email layouts are fixed files, never built from user input.

asvs.proves: CR/LF and header-like sequences are stripped from user-influenced mail fields and templates are loaded from disk only, so mail header injection is prevented.

controls.title: Background jobs declared in code, locked against overlap, no user input in schedules
controls.description: Scheduled jobs are listed in the code, run one at a time using a lock in the database, and their timing can never be set by a user.

asvs.proves: Jobs are declared in a registry, take a lock_until lease before running and never accept user input for schedules or commands.

sbd.proves: Jobs are retried safely at-least-once with overlap protection so a failed run cannot cascade.
Scheduled jobs use a database lease so exactly one runner executes a job at a time.

controls.title: API keys: random, hashed at rest, header-only, scoped, rate limited, revocable
controls.description: Keys for other programs are long random strings stored only as hashes, must be sent in a header (never in the address), only work on API routes, are limited per key and can be revoked.

asvs.proves: API keys are accepted only as Authorization: Bearer; a key in the query string is rejected with 400 and never logged.
Key requests act as the key's owner on routes tagged kind api with auth user, and revoked keys are refused.
Keys are sk_<prefix>_<32 CSPRNG bytes base64url> stored as HMAC-SHA256(TOKEN_HMAC_KEY, key) with only the prefix in clear.

controls.title: Reference feature switched off in production
controls.description: The built-in example feature used for learning and testing is not mounted when the app runs for real.

asvs.proves: The _example feature only mounts with EXAMPLE_FEATURE=1, which the config scanner flags in production.

controls.title: Locked dependencies, no install scripts, update policy and software inventory
controls.description: The exact versions of every package are locked and tested, packages cannot run scripts during installation, a document states how quickly vulnerable packages must be updated, and a full inventory (SBOM) is produced.

asvs.proves: docs/dependencies.md, regenerated from package-lock.json, lists every dependency with the remediation SLA table.
package-lock.json is present and .npmrc sets ignore-scripts=true, so installs are reproducible and cannot run arbitrary scripts.
A CycloneDX SBOM is generated from the lockfile for every build.

sbd.proves: Pinned dependencies and an SBOM reduce the risk of unexpected supply-chain changes.

controls.title: Data classification with per-class controls and retention; retention job
controls.description: A generated document lists what kinds of information the app holds, how each is protected and how long it is kept. When a retention period is set, a job deletes or pseudonymises old records.

asvs.proves: docs/data-protection.md, regenerated from the design profile and entity sensitive fields, documents each data class and its controls.
docs/data-protection.md states the retention period and deletion path per data class.
With RETENTION_MONTHS set, the retention job deletes or pseudonymises records past the period.

sbd.proves: Data is classified with an owner and per-class controls in docs/data-protection.md.
A retention policy is documented and, when configured, enforced by the retention job and the account deletion path.

controls.title: No sensitive data in web addresses; sensitive fields redacted
controls.description: Passwords, keys and other sensitive values are never passed in a page address, where they would end up in browser history and logs, and are redacted from the log.

asvs.proves: Credentials and secrets are never accepted from the query string and never appear in logs or URLs.
Sensitive fields are redacted from logs and excluded from GET parameters by the SAST rule.

controls.title: Request timeouts, health and readiness checks, graceful shutdown
controls.description: Slow or stuck connections are cut off, the app reports whether it is healthy and ready, and it finishes in-flight work before stopping.

asvs.proves: Header (10 s), request (30 s) and keep-alive (5 s) timeouts are set on the server so stalled clients cannot hold resources.

sbd.proves: Timeouts, /healthz, /readyz and graceful shutdown on SIGTERM are implemented; failover is not applicable locally.

controls.title: Idempotency keys on JSON API changes; unique constraints
controls.description: If a program retries a request that creates something, the app recognises the retry and does not create it twice. Database rules prevent duplicate records.

sbd.proves: JSON API mutations honour the Idempotency-Key header by replaying the stored response, and updates use optimistic concurrency on updated_at.
Unique constraints and idempotent handlers keep data consistent under retries.

controls.title: API reference and OpenAPI description generated from the route registry
controls.description: A machine-readable description of every route, with who may call it and what it accepts, is generated from the code.

sbd.proves: docs/openapi.json and docs/api.md are generated from the route registry, giving every route an explicit contract.
The API documentation is regenerated from code, so it cannot drift from the running app.

controls.title: Incident response plan, security contact and deployment guide
controls.description: The app ships with a plain-language plan for what to do when something goes wrong, who to contact, and how to deploy safely.

sbd.proves: docs/incident-response.md exists and docs/SECURITY.md names the security contact; rehearsal still requires an owner attestation.
The deployment guide and SECURITY.md state the regulatory hints and contact for the data classes in use.

controls.title: Security test suite present and passing
controls.description: The app comes with automated tests for its security controls. They must exist for every area and pass before a build is credited.

sbd.proves: ASVS-aligned security tests exist for every area in tests/security and run with node --test.
Negative tests (denied access, rate limits, CSRF, validation) are part of the suite and verifiable by DAST.

controls.title: Listens on the local machine only by default; outside access needs explicit configuration
controls.description: Out of the box the app only answers on the computer it runs on. Opening it to the local network or the internet is a deliberate setting, and outgoing connections are blocked unless allow-listed.

sbd.proves: The app binds 127.0.0.1 unless BIND_LAN=1 and egress is deny-by-default, enforcing browser / app / data / vendor trust zones.
Loopback-only binding means no network path exists by default; TLS for LAN or internet is a deployment step.

conventions: SC-01 Register every route with defineRoute() from src/security/routes.ts and give it an explicit auth value ('public', 'user' or 'role:<name>'). A route without auth does not exist: the app refuses to start.
SC-02 Give every route strict zod schemas for params, query and body (z.strictObject / .strict()). Body schemas are required for POST, PUT and PATCH. Handlers read only req.valid.{params,query,body}.
SC-03 All database access goes through the helpers in src/db/index.ts (q, run, get, all, withTransaction) with bound parameters. Never build SQL from strings.
SC-04 Return DTOs, never raw rows: every entity module exports toPublicDto, toOwnerDto and toAdminDto built with pick()/omit() from src/lib/dto.ts.
SC-05 For records that belong to a user, declare owner: { entity, param, ownerField } on the route so requireOwner enforces ownership (admins bypass only where the registry says so).

SC-06 In EJS views use <%= %> for data. <%- %> only for nonce, csrfToken or safeHtml(). No inline scripts or inline event handlers: scripts live in public/js/features/ and are loaded by the layout with the nonce.
SC-07 Never use eval, new Function, node:vm or child_process.
SC-08 Do not add dependencies. Import only express, zod, ejs, pino, node:* and the template's own modules.
SC-09 Read secrets and settings only through config from src/config.ts, never process.env directly and never with literal fallbacks.
SC-10 Log through logger (src/lib/logger.ts) and events.emit (src/security/events.ts). Never console.log. Never log passwords, tokens, cookies, keys or sensitive entity fields.
SC-11 Outbound HTTP only through outboundFetch in src/lib/http-client.ts (allow-listed hosts, timeouts, manual redirects).
SC-12 Handle file uploads and downloads only through the uploads module (src/features/uploads).
SC-13 Call the AI model only through the ai module (src/features/ai); prompt.ts and tools.ts are the only editable files there.
SC-14 Redirect only with safeRedirect from src/security/redirect.ts.
SC-15 Wrap multi-row writes in withTransaction.
SC-16 New migrations are src/db/migrations/1NN_<name>.sql (numbers >= 100), additive only; every list query has a LIMIT.
SC-17 Write tests/features/<name>.test.ts for every generated feature with at least: anonymous denied, wrong role denied, validation rejects bad input, owner check. Use tests/helpers/app.ts.
SC-18 Add a routes.manifest.json entry { method, path, auth, roles, owner, entity, kind, csrf } for every route you register.
SC-19 Store sensitive entity fields with encryptField/decryptField from src/db/field-crypto.ts.
SC-20 Never modify protected paths (see protectedPaths). Only writablePaths may change.
SC-21 Use erasable TypeScript only (no enum, namespace, parameter properties) and explicit .ts extensions on relative imports; import type for types.
SC-22 Never put sensitive data in GET parameters or URLs; sensitive values travel in POST bodies only.
SC-23 Enforce a per-user quota on user-created records inside a transaction, as src/features/_example does.
SC-24 Multi-step flows keep their state on the server (session or a table), never in hidden fields or query strings.
SC-25 Every generated code file starts with the provenance header comment: // Generated by SecureVibe (AI-generated) — run <runId>
